title: Master of the senses
hook: the last lines of the book are about the one who wrote it
carry: the self holds the reins of the senses
tomorrow: a prince comes home and nothing matters to him. what's wrong?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kama Sutra's ethics chapter let the critics of dharma have their pigeon, and answered with a farmer's seed. Today, the book's very last lines.
screen: `A SEED IN THE GROUND IS REAL TOO.`

segments.voice: Midnight. One more video, then one more, and the thumb seems to be running the show. Somewhere in there a question floats up: who's actually in charge here? The Kama Sutra's last lines take up that question, and they aren't about love at all. They're about the man who wrote the book, and how he says he worked.
screen: `ONE MORE VIDEO.` → `WHO'S IN CHARGE HERE?` → `THE LAST LINES ARE ABOUT THE AUTHOR.`

segments.voice: Vatsyayana says he gathered what older teachers had written, and composed this book while keeping himself restrained, in deep meditation, for the good of the world. Then he says what it is not. It isn't meant, he says, merely as an instrument for satisfying desire. Someone who truly understands it keeps dharma, artha and kama all in view, pays attention to the customs of the people around them, and so gains mastery over the senses. Mastery. That's where a book on pleasure says it's headed. The book's name for the three aims held together is trivarga, the group of three. So the two ends of the book match. The opening sets kama inside the trivarga, beside right living and wealth. The closing says the point of knowing kama is to be master of the senses, not their servant. And mastery here doesn't mean shutting the senses off. Hindus have an old picture for it, from the Katha Upanishad: the body is a chariot, the senses are its horses, the mind is the reins, and the self rides inside. A good driver doesn't get rid of the horses. He holds the reins. The middle of the book this path leaves on the shelf. But the frame says how its author asked the whole to be read: as one part of a life, held by someone still in charge.
screen: `WRITTEN IN RESTRAINT AND MEDITATION.` · `NOT MERELY FOR DESIRE.` · `ALL THREE AIMS IN VIEW.` · `KATHA UPANISHAD: SENSES ARE HORSES, MIND THE REINS.` · then, large: `MASTER OF THE SENSES, NOT THEIR SERVANT.`

segments.voice: If there's something small to eat nearby, a raisin, a square of chocolate, a slice of fruit, hold it and smell it first, and don't eat yet. Notice the pull, and let it be there without obeying it. Then take one slow bite and taste all of it. If there's nothing to eat, do the same with a sip of water.
The Kama Sutra's ethics chapter, closed by the book's last lines: knowing all three aims, and so mastering the senses.
screen: `THE KAMA SUTRA'S ETHICS CHAPTER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Carry this: the self holds the reins of the senses. That closes the Kama Sutra.

screen: `DAY 1600 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY DOES NOTHING MATTER TO THE PRINCE?`

fork.setup: on a Navratri fast, a friend asks: 'if hinduism says pleasure is fine, why give up foods for nine days?' by the Kama Sutra's last lines, what's the answer?
options: the fast trains the reins: mastery of the senses, not hatred of food.
food is bad, so the fast proves you're better than it.
no reason; it's only a custom nobody explains.
fork.reveal: the book's goal is mastery of the senses, not their removal. in the Katha Upanishad's picture, the senses are horses and the driver holds the reins; many Hindus see a fast as practice with the reins.

original.note: Sanskrit trivarga, the group of three: dharma, artha and kama held together.

Vatsyayana.meaning: the author of the Kama Sutra

trivarga.meaning: the group of three: dharma, artha and kama

artha.meaning: wealth and a living; one of the three aims

kama.meaning: pleasure and love; one of the three aims of life
